title: The Latticework
dek: The machine behind the machine. How I try to understand things, and the named ways I know I get it wrong.

p: A single discipline gives you one lens and a strong incentive to see every problem through it. A latticework of models from several fields — physics, biology, economics, psychology, engineering — gives you the ability to look at a problem six ways and notice which lens actually fits.
This is Munger's argument and I have not found a better one. The cost is that you must learn the models well enough to be genuinely fluent, because a half-remembered model is worse than none.

entries.h: The map is not the territory
p: Every model is a compression, and compression is lossy by definition. The failure mode is not using models; it is forgetting which parts your model threw away, and then being surprised when reality behaves according to the discarded parts.
Practical version: for any model I am relying on, I want to name what it is ignoring.

entries.h: The brain was not built for truth
p: It was built for speed, social standing and survival. The named biases — availability, confirmation, sunk cost, anchoring, narrative — are not moral failings; they are the documented bugs of a fast system doing what it was optimised to do.
You cannot patch them out. Naming them lets you catch them in the act, which is a much weaker but genuinely real intervention.

Almost all of the difference between clever and wise is one question asked enough times. First-order thinking stops at the immediate effect. Second- and third-order thinking asks what the immediate effect causes, and what people do once they notice.
Most bad policy, bad product decisions and bad personal choices are first-order-correct.

entries.h: Events sit on patterns; patterns sit on structure
p: What you see are events. Underneath are patterns over time, underneath those is the structure generating them, and underneath that are the mental models that built the structure. Intervening at the event level almost never holds.
The intuition that everything connects has a formal name — systems thinking — and the payoff is in learning to intervene one level lower than feels natural.
Outcomes in most interesting domains are power-law distributed, not normal: a tiny fraction of inputs produce most of the result. Intuitions trained on averages are actively misleading here.
The operational form is the bottleneck: in any system, one constraint governs throughput, and effort spent anywhere else is decoration.

entries.h: Waiting for certainty is itself a decision, and usually a bad one
p: You will never have full information. The tools that work are unglamorous: expected value over outcomes rather than over stories, base rates before specifics, explicit confidence rather than binary belief, and — most useful — sorting decisions by reversibility.
Reversible decisions should be made fast and cheaply. Irreversible ones deserve the time everyone spends on the reversible ones.

entries.h: A question is a model you can carry in a pocket
p: A few questions collected from the sources, kept because they reorganise a problem on contact. What is obvious to me that is not obvious to others? What would make me stop working on this — and if the answer is nothing, is this the thing? Where do I have a specific, unfair advantage, and am I actually standing on it? Is the variation I am explaining over time, or across places?
None of these are mine. That is rather the point of a latticework.
entries.src: after Richard Thaler, Christian Cacioppo, Chris Camillo

entries.h: A model you nod at is worthless
p: The transfer from page to reflex happens through use, not through reading. What has actually worked for me is a short checklist run on real decisions until the questions start arriving unprompted.

heur.b: What is this model throwing away?
heur.s: Every compression discards something. Name it.

heur.b: And then what? And then what?
heur.s: Twice, minimum. Three times on anything involving other people's incentives.
If yes, decide in minutes. If no, take the week.

heur.b: What would change my mind, specifically?
heur.s: If there is no answer, I do not have a position — I have an attachment.
